data:
keen-pbr helps you send selected sites and services through a VPN while the rest of your traffic keeps using the normal connection.
New here? Start with Getting Started for package installation and first setup, or jump straight to Quick Start if keen-pbr is already installed.
For the full configuration reference, see Configuration.
If you want to understand how lists, rules and outbounds fit together, see Concepts.
Commands and service signals are described in CLI, HTTP integration in REST API.
If something is not working, see Troubleshooting or FAQ.
Building packages and compiling from source are covered in Developer.
You can support keen-pbr development at Support This Project.
What changed in each keen-pbr release, and what to do when you upgrade.
data.fixes#Fixes: urltest and icmptest groups accepted members of any type, although only interface and table work. Other types now fail config validation. A blackhole member was never selected: keen-pbr skips it and logs a warning. You do not need it to block traffic: when no link works, traffic is blocked anyway. Automatic list updates stopped after the first list change that affected routing. They now keep running on schedule. New devices could not get an address over DHCP when a route rule matched all UDP traffic. With inbound_interfaces set, the router’s own traffic skipped route rules even when it should have matched. When several DNS rules named the same list, only the first rule’s server was used. Now dnsmasq gets the servers of every rule and switches between them. On Keenetic, a burst of route changes on WAN DHCP renewal could leave routing built from a half-updated table. After a power loss a list cache file could be left empty. keen-pbr status reported every urltest and icmptest rule as an error. The Web UI dropped conntrack_on_switch, strict_enforcement_action and the urltest probe timeout when saving an outbound. A DNS server with detour through a tunnel did not answer: queries entered the tunnel with the ISP address. They now use the tunnel address (for servers with an IPv4 address).
data.upgrading-from-33x#Upgrading from 3.3.x:
After the upgrade, dnsmasq management stays on, as in 3.3.x. If you do not need it, turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration in the Web UI (General > Settings > Local DNS server management) and follow the rollback steps: Keenetic, OpenWrt, Debian. Without it, DNS rules and default DNS servers stop working.
Keenetic. keen-pbr 3.3.x installed dnsmasq-full as a dependency, and opkg may remove it during the upgrade. If it is gone, the Web UI opens a window with two ways out: install it again with opkg install dnsmasq-full, or turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration.
Check after the upgrade:
Keenetic: kernel modules. Domains are now detected by interception. Install the Netfilter Subsystem Kernel Modules component if you have not. Then open the status page in the Web UI and run the DNS check. Keenetic: iptables only. The Keenetic build always uses iptables. A config with daemon.firewall_backend: "nftables" or strategy: "balance" does not pass validation there. Debian 11 (bullseye) is no longer supported. Changed defaults. daemon.clear_dynamic_sets_on_apply is now false: domain addresses survive a config apply. A list’s ttl_ms is now a lower bound; the upper bound is intercept.max_ttl_ms. iproute.process_router_traffic is false: route rules apply to devices in your network, not to the router’s own traffic. --log-target is both for every command. The packaged service files pass --log-target syslog. Ignored fields. dns.system_resolver, dns.dns_test_server (use intercept.dns.marker) and daemon.resolver_ready_timeout_seconds no longer do anything; the log warns if they are set. The old outbounds, candidates and weight fields in outbound_groups are replaced by members; old configs keep working, and keen-pbr rewrites them once, keeping a copy in .bak-pre-members. New field version. It records which keen-pbr version the config was written for. keen-pbr sets it when you save from the Web UI. Keep it if you edit the file by hand. DNS check domain. To check DNS by hand, run nslookup check.keen-pbr.fyi instead of nslookup check.keen.pbr. See Troubleshooting. If you use scripts or other programs with keen-pbr:
keen-pbr resolver-config-hash does nothing and always succeeds. keen-pbr generate-resolver-config takes dnsmasq instead of dnsmasq-ipset and dnsmasq-nftset. keen-pbr status exits with code 1 when any check failed or any issue is an error. GET /api/dns/test?show=all (and show=full) works only with API authentication turned on. New endpoints: GET /metrics, GET /api/health/issues, GET /api/config/defaults. GET /api/status/events also sends issues, routing health, authentication state and config changes.
data.whats-new#What\u0026rsquo;s new: Domain lists work without a resolver setup. keen-pbr reads DNS replies passing through the router and the site names in TLS, HTTP and QUIC connections, and fills the sets of your lists itself. The first connection to a site already takes the right route. If the kernel lacks a feature, only that part (DNS or connections) is turned off, and the status page says why. See DNS. dnsmasq is optional. It is needed only for separate DNS servers for some lists or for your own default DNS servers. See Do I need dnsmasq?. keen-pbr can pick the dnsmasq instance, shows its state in the Web UI and repairs it when it loses the config. New commands: keen-pbr dnsmasq detect and keen-pbr dnsmasq remove. Load balancing across several links (strategy: "balance" in a urltest outbound) with a weight for each link. A connection stays on the link it started on. It is not available in the Keenetic build. See Multi-WAN Load Balancing. Automatic gateway detection for interface outbounds ("gateway": "auto"), and editing the default gateway in the Web UI. See interface. All internet traffic through failover or balancing: the new default_gateway route rule condition (nftables only). See Route rules. New Web UI: compact overview, live table of current requests, request log with explained badges and filters, a diagnostics panel (kernel checks first), redesigned outbound editor, updates over a live stream instead of polling, better mobile layout, and a settings page that shows the daemon’s defaults. Health checks warn about missing NAT or strict rp_filter on balanced links, foreign fwmarks that overlap fwmark.mask, and missing iptables extensions. keen-pbr status shows the same issue list as the Web UI. Prometheus endpoint GET /metrics with probe latency, link selection, list updates, balance and interception counters, plus a Grafana dashboard and alert examples. See REST API. keen-pbr test-routing takes packet criteria (protocol, ports, addresses, DSCP) and runs in the daemon, the same way as the routing test in the Web UI. The router’s own traffic is left alone by default. Route rules apply to devices in your network. To include the router, set iproute.process_router_traffic to true. See iproute. The default config ships a rule that keeps local networks out of tunnels. The “What’s new?” button in the Web UI opens this page. Lists that failed to download at start are retried in the background. Removing the package also removes leftover firewall rules and dnsmasq files.

data:
keen-pbr can run the service, inspect live routing state, download list data, and test routing decisions.
The status, download and test-routing commands talk to the running service. If the service is not running, they fail with exit code 1. Start the service first (on a router it starts with the system).
data.--use-raw-prerouting#\u003ccode\u003e--u:
This flag is mainly for Keenetic / NetCraze. The firmware periodically rebuilds the mangle firewall table, and keen-pbr’s rules briefly disappear. With this flag keen-pbr puts the rules for IPv4 traffic passing through the router into the raw table, which the firmware does not rebuild. IPv6 has a separate flag, --use-raw6-prerouting.
On Keenetic / NetCraze the start script sets these flags. The mode is set with KEEN_PBR_RAW_PREROUTING in /opt/etc/keen-pbr/defaults:
Value What it does auto (default) Checks separately for IPv4 and IPv6 whether raw works, and uses it if so; otherwise mangle disable Always use mangle enable Require raw for IPv4 and IPv6. If raw is unavailable, the service does not start ipv4-only, ipv6-only Require raw for one address family only Restart the service after changing it. The practical difference between the modes is described in Keenetic / NetCraze installation.
To check whether raw is available:
ls -l "/lib/modules/$(uname -r)/iptable_raw.ko" ls -l "/lib/modules/$(uname -r)/ip6table_raw.ko" grep -x raw /proc/net/ip_tables_names grep -x raw /proc/net/ip6_tables_names iptables -t raw -S ip6tables -t raw -S
data.commands#Commands: Command Description service Start the routing service in the foreground. status Show service, outbound, routing, firewall and kernel health, then the issue list the web UI overview shows, and exit. Exits with 1 when any check failed or any issue is an error. download [--reload] Download all URL-backed lists into the cache and exit. With --reload the service applies the lists that changed right away. generate-resolver-config dnsmasq Print the dnsmasq configuration for per-list DNS servers. hash-password [--update] Create a password hash for logging in to the web UI and API. dnsmasq detect [--json] List dnsmasq instances, their DNS endpoints and the instance keen-pbr uses. dnsmasq remove Restart one dnsmasq instance without keen-pbr’s config. test-routing [packet options] Compare expected and actual routing for the given IP or domain. The daemon runs the check, the same way as the routing test in the web UI.
data.dnsmasq-detect-and-remove#\u003ccode\u00:
Inspect and clean up the dnsmasq integration without the daemon. Neither command needs the control socket.
keen-pbr dnsmasq detect [--json] keen-pbr dnsmasq remove detect lists every dnsmasq instance the platform hook reports: whether it runs, its DNS endpoint and how it was confirmed, listening sockets, whether keen-pbr’s drop-in is installed and which configuration it loaded, and any problem. The last line tells which instance keen-pbr selected and how (explicit, adopted or automatic), or why it could not choose.
dnsmasq hook: /usr/lib/keen-pbr/dnsmasq-hook.sh (platform openwrt, binary /usr/sbin/dnsmasq) uci:cfg01411c [selected: adopted] running: yes (pid 1842) enabled: yes endpoint: 127.0.0.1:53 (stamp_verified) listeners: udp+tcp 0.0.0.0:53, udp+tcp [::]:53 keen-pbr: installed, loaded hash 3f2a9c0e1b7d4a55c6e8f0a1b2c3d4e5 conf-dir: /tmp/dnsmasq.cfg01411c.d (included) problem: none Selection: uci:cfg01411c (adopted) --json prints the same data as one JSON object (selected, selection, error_code, message, warnings, instances[]). Exit code 0 when an instance is selected and has no problem, 1 otherwise. If the choice is ambiguous, the output ends with a hint to set dns.dnsmasq_instance. remove restarts one instance so that it stops using keen-pbr’s config; on OpenWrt it also returns the server list moved aside. Use it when detect shows an instance that still runs keen-pbr’s config after you switched the integration off.
Must run as root. Exit code 64 for a missing or invalid selector. If the integration is still enabled for this instance, the command prints a note: the daemon may apply its config to dnsmasq again on its next sync. Disable the integration first.

bashkeen-pbr download The command prints the service’s answer as one JSON line. refreshed_lists holds the lists that were updated, changed_lists those whose content changed:
{"ok":true,"protocol_version":2,"request_id":"cli-download","result":{"changed_lists":["google"],"failed_lists":[],"refreshed_lists":["google"],"reloaded":false}} If a list fails to download, the command prints an error and exits with code 1.
Compare expected and actual routing:
bashkeen-pbr test-routing google.com Example output:
Target: google.com Resolved IPs: 2001:4860:4860::8888, 142.250.74.14 IP | List Match | Expected Outbound | Actual Outbound | Status --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 2001:4860:4860::8888 | google (via google.com) | corp_vpn | corp_vpn | OK 142.250.74.14 | google (via google.com) | corp_vpn | corp_vpn | OK By default only list membership is checked. To also match rules that use ports, protocol, source address or DSCP, describe the packet:
Flag Description --proto Packet protocol. --src-addr Source address of the client sending the packet. --src-port Source port. --dest-port Destination port. --dscp <0-63> DSCP value. A packet without --dscp is treated as DSCP 0. bashkeen-pbr test-routing google.com --proto tcp --dest-port 443 --src-addr 192.168.1.10 If a rule depends on a field you did not give (for example src_addr), that IP shows (unknown).
data.generate-resolver-config-dnsmasq#\u003cc:
When dns.resolver_integration: "dnsmasq" is enabled, this command prints the dnsmasq configuration built by keen-pbr. Lists are taken from the cache only; nothing is downloaded. It contains domain-to-server mappings, DNS rebinding protection exceptions, and fallback servers.
Usage:
keen-pbr generate-resolver-config dnsmasq Output: Dnsmasq configuration directives.
# Generated by keen-pbr - do not edit manually address=/use-application-dns.net/ server=192.168.1.1 # List: ai_services server=/openai.com/www.openai.com/.../1.1.1.1 rebind-domain-ok=/openai.com/www.openai.com/... Behavior:
Always exits with status 0, even on errors; errors are printed as # keen-pbr: ... comment lines. When resolver_integration: "none" (default), or the config cannot be read, the output is only the server= lines from dnsmasq-fallback.conf; the dynamic sets are filled by interception. With "dnsmasq" and no fallback servers, those server= lines are added to the output. dnsmasq reads the config via this command (see conf-script=keen-pbr generate-resolver-config dnsmasq in the drop-in ).
data.hash-password#\u003ccode\u003ehash-passw:
Creates a password hash for logging in to the web UI and API. The command asks for the password twice.
keen-pbr hash-password keen-pbr hash-password --update Without --update the command prints Password hash: , which you paste into api.authentication.password_hash yourself. With --update it writes api.enabled: true, api.authentication.enabled: true and the hash into config.json. Then restart the service: Restart the keen-pbr service for authentication changes to take effect.
data.options#Options: Flag Description --config Path to the JSON config file. Works only with the service command. --log-level Log verbosity: error, warn, info, verbose, or debug. --log-target External log destination: stderr, syslog, or both. Defaults to both for every command. The packaged service files (systemd, OpenWrt procd, Keenetic init script) pass --log-target syslog so logs are not duplicated when stdout/stderr are also captured by the init system. --pid-file Path to the PID file (the file holding the service’s process number). Replaces daemon.pid_file from the config; service only. --crash-report Where to write the report about the last crash. Defaults to /tmp/keen-pbr-crash.log. --no-api Disable the REST API even if enabled in config. --use-raw-prerouting Opt in to raw-table IPv4 forwarded-traffic classification; available only with iptables. --use-raw6-prerouting Opt in to raw-table IPv6 forwarded-traffic classification; available only with iptables. --version Print version and exit. --help Print help and exit.
data.signals#Signals:
You can control the running keen-pbr service with signals:
Signal Action SIGUSR1 Rebuild routes and firewall rules SIGHUP Re-read config.json and apply it again. Does not work in the keen-pbr-headless build SIGTERM / SIGINT Graceful shutdown Example: re-read the config with SIGHUP:
bashkill -HUP $(cat /var/run/keen-pbr.pid)
data.usage#Usage: Usage: keen-pbr [options] Options: --config Path to JSON config file (default: ) --log-level Log level: error, warn, info, verbose, debug (default: info) --log-target Log destination: stderr, syslog, or both (default: both) --pid-file Override daemon.pid_file when running the service command --crash-report Last-crash report path (default: /tmp/keen-pbr-crash.log) --no-api Disable REST API at runtime --use-raw-prerouting Use raw PREROUTING for IPv4 forwarded traffic (iptables only) --use-raw6-prerouting Use raw PREROUTING for IPv6 forwarded traffic (iptables only) --version Show version and exit --help Show this help and exit Commands: service Start the routing service (foreground) status Show routing/firewall status and exit download Download all configured lists to cache and exit test-routing [packet options] Test expected vs actual routing for an IP or domain --proto Packet protocol --src-addr Packet source address --src-port Packet source port --dest-port Packet destination port --dscp <0-63> Packet DSCP (default: 0) generate-resolver-config dnsmasq Print the dnsmasq config generated from dns.rules/dns.fallback (cached lists only; used as dnsmasq conf-script, always exits 0) dnsmasq detect [--json] List dnsmasq instances, their DNS endpoints and which one keen-pbr uses dnsmasq remove Restart one dnsmasq instance without keen-pbr's generated config (OpenWrt: also return the moved servers) hash-password [--update] Generate an authentication password hash; --update writes config.json The config file is usually /etc/keen-pbr/config.json on OpenWrt and Debian, and /opt/etc/keen-pbr/config.json on Keenetic / NetCraze.

data: You do not need this page for a normal setup. It explains how keen-pbr decides where traffic goes.
data.dns#DNS:
Domain-based routing needs no DNS server setup. dnsmasq, the Keenetic DNS proxy or any other resolver keeps working as before. keen-pbr learns the addresses of listed sites from DNS replies and from site names in connections that pass through the router.
If some lists need different DNS servers, for example to get CDN addresses for the right region, use per-list DNS servers (via dnsmasq).
See DNS.
data.fwmark-and-conntrack#fwmark and conntrac:
You will meet these two words in logs and search results when something goes wrong. You normally do not need to configure them.
fwmark is a numeric tag on a packet. keen-pbr puts it on traffic from your lists, and the tag tells the router which outbound to send the packet to. Each outbound has its own tag from the range set in the fwmark setting. conntrack is the router’s table of open connections. It keeps all packets of one connection on the same path. When a connection has to move to another channel, keen-pbr clears its entry in this table and the device opens the connection again.
data.lists#Lists:
A list is a set of domains, IP addresses and subnets (CIDR ranges such as 192.168.0.0/16). It can be built from several sources:
URL: the list is downloaded from the internet and refreshed on a schedule; File on the device: the list is read from a file on the router; Domains / IPs: you write the addresses directly in the config. For domains you do not need to know IP addresses. keen-pbr learns the addresses of listed sites when devices on your network open them, and keeps them for a limited time. After you change lists, clear the DNS cache on your device: otherwise it may connect to a site by an old address that keen-pbr does not know yet.
See Lists.
data.outbounds#Outbounds:
An outbound is a channel traffic goes through. There are six types:
Type What it does interface Sends traffic through the chosen network interface, for example a VPN. You can also set IPv4 and IPv6 gateways table Sends traffic along one of the router’s routing tables. Table 254 is the normal internet path through your provider blackhole Drops the traffic, that is, blocks it ignore Leaves the traffic as is: it goes the usual way and the rules below it are not checked urltest Picks the best of several channels: checks them with an HTTP request and takes the one with the lowest latency or spreads connections between them. An unstable channel is temporarily excluded icmptest Same as urltest, but channels are checked with ping ( ICMP ) ignore is for exceptions. For example, a “home network → ignore” rule is placed above the general VPN rule so local traffic does not enter the tunnel.
See Outbounds.
data.routing-rules#Routing rules:
A rule links conditions to an outbound. Conditions can be combined:
Lists: the address is in one of the given lists; Protocol: tcp or udp; DSCP: a traffic priority tag; Source IP and Destination IP: an address or subnet ( CIDR ), optionally negated; Source port and Destination port: a single port, a list or a range. If a rule has several conditions, traffic must match all of them. Rules are checked from top to bottom, and the first matching rule wins. Traffic that matches no rule goes the usual way.
See Routing rules.
data.the-idea-lists-rules-outbounds#The idea::
The easiest comparison is a post office sorting letters.
A list is an address book. One book holds the sites you want to open through a VPN, another holds addresses to block. A routing rule is a sorting instruction: “send letters from this book along this route”. Instructions are read from top to bottom, and the first one that fits wins. An outbound is a delivery route: a VPN interface, your normal provider connection, or “throw the letter away”. A letter whose address is in no book goes the usual way.
For example, you have two books, streaming (streaming services) and work (work sites). The instructions are:
Addresses from local_networks (your home network) are not sent anywhere and stay inside the network. Addresses from work go through the work VPN. Addresses from streaming go through a second VPN. Everything else goes directly through your provider.

data:
keen-pbr reads its settings from one JSON config file.
Common config file locations:
Keenetic / NetCraze: /opt/etc/keen-pbr/config.json OpenWrt: /etc/keen-pbr/config.json Debian: /etc/keen-pbr/config.json If you installed the full package, configure keen-pbr in the Web UI: it writes the config for you, so you do not need to edit the file. If you installed keen-pbr-headless (no Web UI), edit the config file. Configuration has four parts:
Outbounds — the channels traffic can take: a VPN, your ISP connection, or a block Lists — the sites and IP ranges you want to route Route Rules — which list goes through which outbound DNS — DNS servers and DNS interception In the Web UI they correspond to the Routing > Outbounds, Routing > Lists, Routing > Routing rules and General > Settings menu items.
data.advanced-configuration#Advanced Configur:
These settings are optional for most users:
Advanced — API, service paths, automatic list refresh, and low-level routing options Full Reference Config — commented config example with every supported config option List names, outbound tags, and DNS server tags must all follow the same convention: ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$ and must be at most 24 characters.
data.practical-example#Practical Example:
This example sends google.com through the VPN (tun0); all other traffic goes the usual way, through the router’s main connection:
{ "outbounds": [ { "type": "interface", "tag": "vpn", "interface": "tun0" } ], "lists": { "my_sites": { "domains": ["google.com"] } }, "route": { "rules": [ { "list": ["my_sites"], "outbound": "vpn" } ] } }

data:
Most users can skip this page.
These settings are for advanced setups and service-level tuning: daemon, api, fwmark, iproute, and lists_autoupdate.
Some of these settings are in the web UI: General > Settings > General, Lists autoupdate and Advanced routing settings. The low-level fields appear after you switch Settings mode to Advanced. This page describes every config.json field; next to a field you will find where it is in the UI.
data.api#api:
Controls the embedded HTTP API server that the web UI runs on.
Field Type Default Description enabled boolean false Enable the HTTP API and the web UI. The config installed by the keen-pbr package already has it on listen string "0.0.0.0:12121" Address and port to listen on max_request_body_bytes integer 1048576 Maximum request body size in bytes. Minimum 1024. read_timeout_seconds integer 15 How many seconds to wait for a request from the client. Minimum 1. write_timeout_seconds integer 15 How many seconds to send a response to the client. Minimum 1. keep_alive_timeout_seconds integer 20 How many seconds to keep a connection open between requests. Minimum 1. authentication object off Password login: enabled and password_hash. With enabled: true the hash is required. Create it with keen-pbr hash-password --update or in the web UI: Security. cors.allowed_origins array — Site addresses (origins) allowed to call the API from a browser, for example "https://router.example". Exact http:// or https:// addresses only, no path or wildcards. config.json{ "api": { "enabled": true, "listen": "0.0.0.0:12121", "max_request_body_bytes": 1048576, "read_timeout_seconds": 15, "write_timeout_seconds": 15, "keep_alive_timeout_seconds": 20, "authentication": { "enabled": false }, "cors": { "allowed_origins": [] } } } Start keen-pbr with --no-api to disable the API regardless of the config. See REST API for endpoint documentation and runtime controls.
data.daemon#daemon:
Controls the PID file path (the file holding the service’s process number), the cache directory, and general routing behaviour.
Field Type Default Description pid_file string — Path to write the PID file. Can be overridden with the --pid-file flag cache_dir string /var/cache/keen-pbr Directory for cached list data firewall_backend string "auto" Which firewall to use: auto (pick automatically), iptables, or nftables clear_dynamic_sets_on_apply boolean false Clear the dynamic sets (domain IP addresses collected from DNS replies and connections) on every config apply or service restart. List refreshes and link switches never clear them. Web UI: Clear learned domain addresses on apply. ipset_hashsize integer absent Optional initial hash table size for ipsets created by the iptables backend (default 1024). Has no effect with nftables. Must be between 1 and 2147483648. Web UI (Advanced mode): IPSet hash table size (ipset hashsize). Changing it recreates the sets and empties the dynamic sets. ipset_maxelem integer absent Optional maximum element count for ipsets created by the iptables backend (default 65536). Has no effect with nftables. Must be between 1 and 4294967295. Web UI: Maximum entries in ipset (ipset maxelem). Changing it recreates the sets and empties the dynamic sets. reuse_static_sets_on_runtime_refresh boolean true Do not refill list sets on SIGUSR1, urltest/icmptest switches and interface state changes: only rules are updated, which is faster. If false, sets are refilled every time. skip_marked_packets boolean true Do not process packets that another program has already marked. Web UI: Skip packets that are already marked. ipv6_enabled boolean true Route IPv6 traffic. When false, IPv6 flows as usual, bypassing keen-pbr. Web UI: Enable IPv6 support. strict_enforcement boolean false If the interface or gateway of an interface outbound is down, do not let its traffic go out through the normal connection: the outbound’s table gets the route from strict_enforcement_action instead. Can be set per outbound. Web UI: Block traffic when an outbound is unavailable (kill-switch). strict_enforcement_action string "unreachable" What to do with traffic under strict_enforcement: unreachable returns an immediate network error; blackhole silently drops packets until the application times out. max_file_size_bytes integer 8388608 (8 MiB) Maximum allowed size in bytes for downloaded remote list content firewall_verify_max_bytes integer 262144 How many bytes of iptables/nft output to read when checking firewall rules (keen-pbr status, status page); 0 means no limit exec_timeout_seconds integer 30 How many seconds to wait for keen-pbr’s helper scripts (for example the dnsmasq script) before stopping them. Minimum 1. exec_kill_grace_seconds integer 2 How many seconds to give a script to exit after it is stopped before it is killed. Minimum 0. config.json{ "daemon": { "pid_file": "/var/run/keen-pbr.pid", "cache_dir": "/var/cache/keen-pbr", "firewall_backend": "auto", "clear_dynamic_sets_on_apply": false, "ipset_hashsize": null, "ipset_maxelem": null, "reuse_static_sets_on_runtime_refresh": true, "skip_marked_packets": true, "ipv6_enabled": true, "strict_enforcement": false, "strict_enforcement_action": "unreachable", "max_file_size_bytes": 8388608, "firewall_verify_max_bytes": 262144, "exec_timeout_seconds": 30, "exec_kill_grace_seconds": 2 } } The cache directory stores downloaded remote lists so they are available if the network is unreachable at startup.
data.failover#Failover:
Rules are checked top to bottom and the first match wins. Two identical rules with different outbounds therefore do not give you a backup: packets never reach the second rule.
If the first outbound’s interface goes down, the result depends on strict_enforcement:
off (the default): traffic falls back to the ISP’s default gateway, bypassing the VPN; on: traffic is blocked (strict_enforcement_action decides how). To switch traffic to a backup link, create one urltest outbound and put both interfaces in it. conntrack_on_switch controls what happens to open connections when urltest moves to a faster link: preserve (the default) keeps them on the old link, delete deletes their conntrack entries, so applications reconnect through the new one. When the selected link stops working, conntrack entries of its connections are always deleted.
data.fwmark#fwmark:
Sets the range of fwmark values. A fwmark is a label keen-pbr puts on a packet so the system sends it to the right routing table (the table holding one outbound’s routes). See fwmark and conntrack.
Field Type Default Description start string "0x00010000" First fwmark value to assign to outbounds. Web UI: fwmark starting value mask string "0x00FF0000" Fwmark bitmask. Web UI: fwmark mask config.json{ "fwmark": { "start": "0x00010000", "mask": "0x00FF0000" } } mask must be a run of hex F digits, for example 0x00FF0000. Outbounds get sequential fwmark values starting from start, within mask.
If other software on your system uses the same fwmark range, adjust start and mask to avoid conflicts.
data.good-to-know#Good to know: With ipv6_enabled: false, IPv6 traffic flows as usual, bypassing keen-pbr. keen-pbr learns domain IPs from ordinary DNS replies passing through the router, even when a client uses a third-party DNS server. If a device uses encrypted DNS ( DoH , DoT ), keen-pbr learns the site’s address only from the connection itself (the server name in TLS, HTTP or QUIC ), and the first connections may bypass the VPN. To avoid this, turn off “secure DNS” on the device and set up DoH/DoT on the router itself. When a learned domain IP expires from a list, new connections take a different route, while connections that are already open keep their route, because their fwmark is stored in conntrack . keen-pbr download downloads lists into the cache. To make the running service use them, run keen-pbr download --reload or restart the service. If keen-pbr stopped after a crash, do not change fwmark.mask before the next start: otherwise it will not recognise its old rules and cannot remove them. If that has already happened, reboot the router.
data.iproute#iproute:
Sets the routing table numbers and the priorities of the ip rule entries that keen-pbr creates for outbounds. An ip rule entry is a rule that picks a routing table by fwmark.
Field Type Default Description table_start integer 150 First routing table ID to allocate for outbounds. Web UI: IP routing table starting value rule_priority_start integer or null table_start Priority of the first ip rule entry; null means the same as table_start process_router_traffic boolean false Apply route rules to traffic of the router itself and collect domain IPs from it. When false, keen-pbr handles only traffic of devices in the network. detour of DNS servers works either way. Web UI (Advanced mode): Process router’s own traffic. config.json{ "iproute": { "table_start": 150, "rule_priority_start": null, "process_router_traffic": false } } Outbounds are assigned sequential table IDs starting from table_start. Check that these IDs do not clash with existing routing tables. Do not start from reserved IDs: 0, 128, 250-260 and everything from 32000. A config with such a table_start fails validation, and reserved IDs are skipped when numbers are allocated.
When keen-pbr stops, it removes only its own routes. Routes added by you or by other software stay in place.
data.lists_autoupdate#lists_autoupdate:
Scheduled refresh of remote lists.
If the lists_autoupdate section is omitted, automatic refresh is disabled. In the web UI: General > Settings > Lists autoupdate.
Field Type Default Description enabled boolean false Enable automatic list refresh. Web UI: Enable lists autoupdate cron string — Refresh schedule: a 5-field cron expression (format below). Web UI: Refresh schedule config.json{ "lists_autoupdate": { "enabled": true, "cron": "0 4 * * 0" } } The cron format: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. The example above runs weekly at 04:00 on Sunday.
If cron is filled in, it is validated even when enabled is false. With enabled: true it is required.
If a remote list could not be downloaded at startup, the daemon keeps retrying it in the background with increasing delays (10 seconds, 30 seconds, 2 minutes, then every 5 minutes) until it succeeds. This does not depend on lists_autoupdate.
You can refresh the lists by hand at any time:
keen-pbr download --reload
data.one-instance-only#One instance only:
Run only one keen-pbr per router. A separate pid_file does not help: a second instance uses the same firewall rule and set names and breaks the first one’s rules.
Put all outbounds and routing rules into one configuration. If you need two independent instances, run them in separate network namespaces.

data: Domains from your lists work without any DNS setup. keen-pbr itself reads the plain DNS replies (port 53) that pass through the router, and the site names at the start of TLS, HTTP and QUIC connections (this is called L7: the site name is read from the first packets of a connection). Details are in DNS interception.
data.add-a-dns-server#Add a DNS server: Open DNS > DNS servers > Add DNS server. Fill in Name, DNS type and Address. In Make requests via Outbound pick an outbound (the channel the traffic goes through: a VPN interface, your ISP or a block) if the server is reachable only through it, for example through the VPN.
data.apply-the-settings#Apply the settings:
Click Apply (or Apply & Restart).
The same settings in config.json:
config.json{ "dns": { "resolver_integration": "dnsmasq", "servers": [ {"tag": "vpn_dns", "address": "1.1.1.1", "detour": "vpn"}, {"tag": "isp_dns", "address": "192.168.1.1"} ], "rules": [ { "list": ["ai_services"], "server": "vpn_dns", "allow_domain_rebinding": false } ], "fallback": ["isp_dns"] } } Several DNS servers for one list. Add one rule per server for the same list. dnsmasq queries all of them, then keeps using the one that answered first, and switches to another when it stops answering.
dnsmasq keeps a separate record (about 200 bytes) for every domain and server pair. Each extra server adds that much memory for every domain of the list, so two servers for a list of 10,000 domains take about 4 MB instead of 2 MB.
data.checks-before-every-restart#Checks befor:
Before restarting dnsmasq, keen-pbr checks the new settings with dnsmasq --test on your current dnsmasq configuration plus keen-pbr’s drop-in . It also checks once that your dnsmasq build supports conf-script.
If a check fails, dnsmasq is not restarted and keeps its old settings. The error code and the dnsmasq output are shown in the web UI and in /api/health/service; fix the problem and apply the configuration again.
Each check runs the config generator, so before each apply the system log shows an extra generate-resolver-config dnsmasq: pid ..., parent ... (dnsmasq) block. This is expected.
data.choosing-the-dnsmasq-instance#Choosing t:
A router can run several dnsmasq instances (on OpenWrt, one per dnsmasq section in /etc/config/dhcp). keen-pbr manages exactly one of them and identifies it by a selector:
Platform Selector Example OpenWrt uci: (name as shown by uci show dhcp) uci:cfg01411c, uci:guest Keenetic ( Entware ) entware:default entware:default Debian systemd:.service systemd:dnsmasq.service The instance is picked in this order:
Explicit: dns.dnsmasq_instance is set. If no such instance exists, keen-pbr reports DNSMASQ_INSTANCE_NOT_FOUND and changes nothing. Adopted: the field is empty and keen-pbr’s drop-in is already installed in exactly one instance. That instance keeps being used. If the drop-in is found in several instances, selection stops with DNSMASQ_INSTANCE_AMBIGUOUS. Automatic: the field is empty, nothing is installed yet, and exactly one enabled instance has DNS (port is not 0). With none, the result is DNSMASQ_NO_DNS_INSTANCE; with several, DNSMASQ_INSTANCE_AMBIGUOUS. When the choice is ambiguous, keen-pbr does not guess: it modifies nothing and leaves existing drop-ins alone. Run keen-pbr dnsmasq detect to see the candidates, then set it under General > Settings > Local DNS server management > dnsmasq instance (or dns.dnsmasq_instance in config.json). If keen-pbr’s drop-in is also installed in an instance that is not selected, detect and the logs show a warning with the command that removes it (keen-pbr dnsmasq remove ).
data.dns-endpoint-detection#DNS endpoint dete: keen-pbr finds the address the selected dnsmasq answers on by itself: it reads the configuration dnsmasq actually loaded and checks the address with a DNS query. If dnsmasq does not serve DNS (port=0, no DNS socket, or another network namespace ), keen-pbr reports an error instead of guessing 127.0.0.1:53.
data.dns-interception#DNS interception:
Interception is on by default. Settings: General > Settings > Domain-based routing. It learns the IP addresses of domains from your lists:
DNS: keen-pbr briefly holds a DNS reply passing through the router, adds its addresses to the list’s set, and only then lets the reply reach the client. This way even the first connection to a site takes the right route. L7: keen-pbr reads the site name at the start of TLS, HTTP and QUIC connections. This helps when a device uses encrypted DNS. Change these settings only when the defaults do not suit you. The intercept section in config.json:
Field Type Default Description enabled boolean true Enable interception (Enable domain-based routing) min_ttl_ms / max_ttl_ms integer 300000 / 86400000 How long to keep an address in a dynamic set: no less and no more than this, in milliseconds (rounded to seconds). Within these bounds the TTL from the DNS reply is used (Minimum TTL, Maximum TTL) dns.enabled boolean true Read DNS replies, UDP and TCP (Intercept DNS server responses) dns.queue_num integer 9053 NFQUEUE number. Change it only if another program uses it (NFQUEUE number) dns.hold_timeout_ms integer 30 How long to wait for addresses to be written before passing the DNS reply to the client. If time runs out, the reply goes out without waiting (DNS hold timeout) dns.marker object check.keen-pbr.fyi / 127.0.0.88 Test domain: if the client’s DNS goes through the router, it resolves to 127.0.0.88 (Marker domain, Marker IPv4 address) l7.enabled boolean true Read site names in connections (Enable L7 interception) l7.nflog_group integer 9054 NFLOG group number. Change it only if another program uses it (NFLOG group) l7.tls / http / quic boolean true Which protocols to read (TLS SNI, HTTP Host, QUIC)
data.do-i-need-dnsmasq#Do I need dnsmasq?:
No, not for routing. Interception works with any resolver: the Keenetic DNS proxy, unbound, dnsmasq or anything else. If your ISP spoofs DNS answers, DoH/DoT on the router is usually enough (DoH and DoT are encrypted DNS).
Yes, if you need one of these two things:
to resolve the domains of some lists through a separate DNS server. For example, a CDN (content delivery network) should answer for your VPN’s region, or the domains resolve only inside the VPN; to set your own default DNS servers for the whole network right in keen-pbr. Both work only through dnsmasq. If neither fits you, leave the Manage dnsmasq configuration switch off. If you upgraded from 3.3.x, the switch is already on: turn it off if you do not need dnsmasq (see Upgrading from 3.3.x).
How to install dnsmasq and how to roll back: Keenetic, OpenWrt, Debian.
data.errors#Errors:
The code is shown in GET /api/health/service (error_code) and in the Web UI. In every case below keen-pbr leaves dnsmasq unrestarted unless the table says otherwise.
Code Meaning What to do DNSMASQ_NO_HOOK This build has no dnsmasq hook. Use a package built for your platform. DNSMASQ_HOOK_FAILED The hook’s inspect call failed or printed something unreadable. Run keen-pbr dnsmasq detect; check that the hook and keen-pbr are from the same version. DNSMASQ_NOT_INSTALLED dnsmasq is not installed. Install dnsmasq (see above), or, if you do not need it, turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration (dns.resolver_integration: "none"). DNSMASQ_NO_DNS_INSTANCE No enabled instance serves DNS. Enable an instance with DNS, or turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration (dns.resolver_integration: "none"). DNSMASQ_INSTANCE_NOT_FOUND dns.dnsmasq_instance names an instance that does not exist. Fix the selector; keen-pbr dnsmasq detect lists valid ones. DNSMASQ_INSTANCE_AMBIGUOUS Several instances qualify. Set dnsmasq instance (dns.dnsmasq_instance). DNSMASQ_NOT_RUNNING The selected instance is not running. Start dnsmasq yourself. keen-pbr never starts it, and re-applies its configuration once dnsmasq runs again. DNSMASQ_DNS_DISABLED The selected instance has port=0. Pick another instance or enable DNS in this one. DNSMASQ_OTHER_NETNS dnsmasq runs in another network namespace . Not supported; run dnsmasq in the router’s main namespace. DNSMASQ_NO_DNS_LISTENER The process runs but owns no DNS socket. Check listen-address, interface and port in the dnsmasq configuration. DNSMASQ_ENDPOINT_UNRESPONSIVE Sockets exist, but none answered a DNS query. Check that dnsmasq works (nslookup example.com 127.0.0.1). Not restarted. DNSMASQ_DROPIN_NOT_LOADED The running dnsmasq does not read the directory keen-pbr’s drop-in goes to (or a conf-dir filter rejects the file name). Add the directory to the conf-dir of that instance, or relax the filter. DNSMASQ_FOREIGN_DROPIN The drop-in file exists but keen-pbr did not write it. Move or delete the file; keen-pbr never overwrites it. DNSMASQ_CONF_SCRIPT_UNSUPPORTED This dnsmasq build does not run conf-script. Install a dnsmasq build with conf-script support (on Keenetic, dnsmasq-full). DNSMASQ_TEST_FAILED Even a minimal configuration fails dnsmasq --test. Run dnsmasq --test by hand and fix what it reports. DNSMASQ_PREFLIGHT_FAILED The current dnsmasq configuration plus keen-pbr’s drop-in fails --test. Read the dnsmasq output in the error detail and fix the configuration. dnsmasq was not touched. DNSMASQ_APPLY_FAILED The hook failed to install the drop-in. See the hook output in the error detail and the system log. DNSMASQ_CONFIG_NOT_LOADED dnsmasq was restarted, but the new configuration did not show up in time. Check the dnsmasq log; apply the configuration again. DNSMASQ_STAMP_MISMATCH dnsmasq serves a different configuration than expected (for example, it was restarted by someone else). keen-pbr repairs this itself within the limits described below. DNSMASQ_REPAIR_PAUSED The automatic repair budget is used up. Find out why dnsmasq loses the configuration, then apply the configuration or restart keen-pbr. DNSMASQ_PROBE_FAILED The process is alive but stopped answering. Check dnsmasq. It is not restarted.
data.field-reference#Field reference:
The dns section in config.json:
Field Type Required Description servers array no DNS server definitions (see above) resolver_integration string no "none" (default) or "dnsmasq". In the Web UI: Manage dnsmasq configuration. dnsmasq_instance string no Selector of the dnsmasq instance to manage: uci: (OpenWrt), entware:default (Keenetic), systemd:.service (Debian). In the Web UI: dnsmasq instance. Empty means automatic selection; needed only when several instances are found. rules array no Rules that map lists to DNS servers (only active when resolver_integration: "dnsmasq") fallback array of string no Tags of upstream DNS servers for queries that match no rule (only active when resolver_integration: "dnsmasq"). In the Web UI: Default upstream DNS servers. If omitted, dnsmasq keeps its own servers and also gets the servers from dnsmasq-fallback.conf. dns_test_server object no Ignored; use intercept.dns.marker Rule (rules[] element):
Field Type Default Description enabled bool true Whether the rule is active list array of string required Names of lists whose domains use this DNS server (Domain lists) server string required DNS server tag (DNS server) allow_domain_rebinding bool false Allow private IP answers (RFC1918, local network addresses) for these domains → rebind-domain-ok in dnsmasq (Allow domain rebinding for these domains). Turn it on only if the list points to internal services.
data.how-it-works#How it works:
One drop-in line in the dnsmasq configuration makes dnsmasq run keen-pbr at every start and get the per-list rules and default DNS servers from it.
With Manage dnsmasq configuration on, dnsmasq is restarted when this data changes (list update, settings change, or once after keen-pbr starts), and only after the checks described in Checks before every restart have passed. With it off, dnsmasq gets the servers from the dnsmasq-fallback.conf file (Keenetic: /opt/etc/keen-pbr/, Debian and OpenWrt: /etc/keen-pbr/). They are added to dnsmasq’s own servers; clear the file to avoid that. On OpenWrt the file is empty by default. With it on but no default DNS servers set, dnsmasq also gets the servers from dnsmasq-fallback.conf.
data.how-to-check-that-dns-goes-through-the-r:
Interception sees only the DNS queries that pass through the router. If a device uses DoH or its own DNS server, keen-pbr can recognise part of the domains only through L7.
Open General > Dashboard and find the DNS interception card. Click Check again. To test another device, click Test from another device and run the shown nslookup command on a computer or phone while the window is open. You can also check by hand on the device:
bashnslookup check.keen-pbr.fyi Answer 127.0.0.88: the device’s DNS queries go through the router, everything works. Any other address: the device bypasses the router or uses encrypted DNS. Turn off secure DNS (DoH) in the browser and the system. No answer: DNS does not work on the device.
data.installation-by-platform#Installation by:
keen-pbr does not install dnsmasq; install it yourself when you need this feature. Step-by-step install and rollback are on the installation pages: Keenetic, OpenWrt, Debian. What keen-pbr changes on each platform:
OpenWrt: install dnsmasq. keen-pbr adds three addnmount entries to the dnsmasq section in /etc/config/dhcp, so that the sandboxed dnsmasq can run keen-pbr. While management is on and default DNS servers are set, keen-pbr takes the servers without a domain out of /etc/config/dhcp; per-domain servers stay. Turning management off or clearing the default servers returns them. Removing the package removes the added entries.
Keenetic (Entware): install dnsmasq-full (replaces the built-in ndnproxy as the LAN resolver). The first time you turn management on, keen-pbr adds a marked block with one conf-script line to /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf. install-recommended-config adds the same block. If dnsmasq is not installed, the status page shows an error.
Debian: install dnsmasq. The first time you turn management on, keen-pbr adds a marked block to /etc/dnsmasq.conf. install-recommended-config adds the same block. If dnsmasq is not installed, the status page shows an error.
Keenetic and Debian also ship install-recommended-config (see the installation pages). It replaces the main dnsmasq config with recommended settings, saves the previous file next to it, and restarts dnsmasq.
data.kernel-requirements#Kernel requirements:
Interception works on most routers. Minimum Linux kernel versions:
Firewall backend DNS interception L7 interception iptables 3.8 2.6.39 nftables 4.1 4.5 Router vendors sometimes strip parts of the kernel, so keen-pbr does not rely on the version number: when the service starts, it checks that everything it needs actually works. If something is missing, only that part of interception is turned off and the rest of keen-pbr keeps working. The result is shown on the status page of the web UI and in GET /api/health/service (the intercept field). The check runs once at startup: if you install missing kernel modules, restart the service.
data.link-the-server-to-lists#Link the server: Open DNS > DNS Rules > Add DNS rule. In Domain lists pick the lists, and in DNS server the server from the previous step.
data.on-stop-disable-or-uninstall#On stop, di: Stopping keen-pbr: dnsmasq is not restarted; per-list DNS servers keep working, also after a dnsmasq or router restart. Disabling the feature (resolver_integration: "none"): keen-pbr restarts dnsmasq, which then uses the servers from dnsmasq-fallback.conf. On OpenWrt the server list returns to /etc/config/dhcp. If you turned it off by editing the config while keen-pbr was stopped, the first start restarts dnsmasq once. See dnsmasq commands. dnsmasq is not running: keen-pbr never starts a stopped dnsmasq. If dnsmasq crashes on a system without a service supervisor ( Entware ), start it manually; keen-pbr re-applies its configuration once dnsmasq is running again. dnsmasq loses the config (restarted with other settings): keen-pbr restarts it at most 3 times (immediately, then after 5 and 10 minutes) and then pauses automatic repair; state in /api/health/service shows reconciling or error with the reason. Applying the configuration or restarting keen-pbr re-arms it. A dnsmasq that is running but does not answer the config check is never restarted. Uninstalling the package: keen-pbr removes its entry from dnsmasq, returns the OpenWrt server list, and restarts dnsmasq. This works even when keen-pbr itself is broken, because the removal scripts never run it. If dnsmasq would be left without any upstream DNS server (it has no-resolv and no server= line of its own), the servers from dnsmasq-fallback.conf stay in a block marked keen-pbr fallback upstream in /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf (Keenetic) or /etc/dnsmasq.conf (Debian). Replace them with your own. Firewall rules left behind by a keen-pbr that crashed are removed as well.
data.per-list-dns-servers-dnsmasq#Per-list DN:
Use this when a CDN should return addresses for your VPN’s region, or when different services need different DNS servers.
Example: AI service domains are resolved through a DNS server behind the VPN. The CDN then returns addresses for the VPN exit country, and the service does not see that you connect from another country (otherwise the account may get banned).
data.set-default-dns-servers-optional#Set def: In the Default upstream DNS servers block click Add default DNS server and pick the servers for all other domains. If the block is empty, dnsmasq uses its usual DNS servers.
data.the-keenetic-dns-type#The \u0026ldquo;Ke:
On Keenetic routers, type: "keenetic" takes the DNS servers from the router’s current settings. You set them in the Keenetic web interface: Network rules > Internet safety > DNS Configuration. If DoT or DoH servers are set there, only they are used.
At most one server may use type: "keenetic". address is not set for it. keen-pbr reads the servers that are not tied to a domain from the System proxy policy. If any of them are encrypted ( DoH /DoT), all encrypted servers are used in order. Otherwise, all plain servers are used in order.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: See Per-list DNS servers do not work.
data.turn-on-dnsmasq-management#Turn on dnsma: Open General > Settings > Local DNS server management and turn on Manage dnsmasq configuration. The DNS servers and DNS Rules pages open only after that.

This page shows one full configuration example with comments, including platform-specific settings marked in the example. Remove settings that are unsupported on your target platform before applying it.
You can write // comments in config.json. Replace sample interfaces, addresses, and file paths with values from your network before applying it.
List names, outbound tags, and DNS server tags must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$ and must be at most 24 characters. config.json{ // keen-pbr version this config was written for (X.Y.Z). // Set automatically when you save from the Web UI; keep it when editing by hand. "version": "3.4.0", // Optional device label shown in the browser title and beneath the keen-pbr logo. // Maximum length: 128 characters. Default: empty (the standard keen-pbr // branding is used). "device_name": "Home router", // General keen-pbr service settings. // All fields in this section are optional. "daemon": { // Path to the PID file (the file holding the service's process number). // Default: no file is written when omitted. "pid_file": "/var/run/keen-pbr.pid", // Directory used for remote-list cache files and cache metadata. // Default: "/var/cache/keen-pbr". "cache_dir": "/var/cache/keen-pbr", // Which firewall to use. // Supported values: "auto", "iptables", "nftables". // Default: "auto". "firewall_backend": "auto", // Do not process packets that another program has already marked (fwmark). // Default: true (also when set to null). "skip_marked_packets": true, // Clear the dynamic sets (domain IPs from DNS replies and connections) on // every config apply or service restart. Default: false (also when set to null). "clear_dynamic_sets_on_apply": false, // Optional initial hash table size for ipsets created by the iptables backend. // Has no effect with nftables. Minimum: 1; maximum: 2147483648. Omit or set // to null to use the ipset default (1024). // Changing it recreates the sets and empties the dynamic sets. "ipset_hashsize": null, // Optional maximum element count for ipsets created by the iptables backend. // Has no effect with nftables. Minimum: 1; maximum: 4294967295. Omit or set // to null to use the ipset default (65536). // Changing it recreates the sets and empties the dynamic sets. "ipset_maxelem": null, // Do not refill list sets on SIGUSR1, urltest/icmptest switches and // interface changes; only rules are updated. Default: true. "reuse_static_sets_on_runtime_refresh": true, // Route IPv6 traffic. Default: true (also when set to null). // If the system has no IPv6 support, keen-pbr logs an error and continues // in IPv4-only mode. "ipv6_enabled": true, // Block traffic when an interface outbound is down instead of letting it // go out through the normal connection. Default: false. "strict_enforcement": false, // What to do with traffic when strict_enforcement applies. // Supported values: "unreachable" (return a network error) or "blackhole" // (silently drop packets). Default: "unreachable". "strict_enforcement_action": "unreachable", // Maximum allowed size for downloaded remote content such as URL-backed lists. // Default: 8388608 bytes (8 MiB). "max_file_size_bytes": 8388608, // How many bytes of iptables/nft output to read when checking firewall rules // (`keen-pbr status`, status page). 0 means no limit. // Default: 262144. "firewall_verify_max_bytes": 262144, // How many seconds to wait for keen-pbr's helper scripts (for example the // dnsmasq script) before stopping them. Minimum: 1. Default: 30. "exec_timeout_seconds": 30, // How many seconds to give a script to exit after it is stopped before it // is killed. Minimum: 0. Default: 2. "exec_kill_grace_seconds": 2 }, // Embedded HTTP API and web UI settings. // WARNING: This section is NOT available in keen-pbr-headless package "api": { // Enable or disable the HTTP API and the web UI. // Default: false. "enabled": true, // Address and port the API server listens on. // Default: "0.0.0.0:12121". "listen": "0.0.0.0:12121", // Maximum request body size in bytes. Minimum: 1024. Default: 1048576. "max_request_body_bytes": 1048576, // How many seconds to wait for an HTTP request from the client. // Minimum: 1. Default: 15.
