The REST API lets scripts and external systems control and monitor keen-pbr. For example:
Prometheus and Grafana show VPN channel health and latency (see GET /metrics). A cron job refreshes lists on a schedule through POST /api/lists/refresh. A script restarts routing through POST /api/service/restart. If you only use the web interface, you can skip this page.
The REST API is available when:
Full package version is installed (keen-pbr, not keen-pbr-headless) The config has api.enabled: true The --no-api flag was not passed at startup
data.balancing-and-marked-packets#Balancing a:
These metrics exist only with the iptables firewall backend. A series with no data is omitted. Counters restart from zero when the firewall rules are rebuilt.
Metric Type Labels Meaning keen_pbr_balance_classifications_total counter outbound, candidate, family = ipv4, ipv6 New connections that a balance group sent through the candidate channel. keen_pbr_skip_marked_packets_total counter family = ipv4, ipv6 Packets keen-pbr skipped because they were already marked (General > Settings > General > Skip packets that are already marked). The “slow write” share is derived from the le="0.025" bucket of keen_pbr_set_write_duration_seconds (writes slower than 25 ms).
Prometheus scrape configuration:
scrape_configs: - job_name: keen-pbr metrics_path: /metrics scrape_interval: 15s static_configs: - targets: ["router.example:12121"] basic_auth: username: admin password_file: /etc/prometheus/keen-pbr-password Example queries:
# ICMP packet loss over 15 minutes, in percent (no data when nothing was sent) 100 * clamp(1 - increase(keen_pbr_probe_packets_received_total[15m]) / (increase(keen_pbr_probe_packets_sent_total[15m]) > 0), 0, 1) # Probe success rate over 15 minutes 100 * increase(keen_pbr_probe_successes_total[15m]) / (increase(keen_pbr_probe_attempts_total[15m]) > 0) # Average and 95th percentile latency per outbound over 1 hour (seconds) avg_over_time(keen_pbr_probe_latency_seconds[1h]) quantile_over_time(0.95, keen_pbr_probe_latency_seconds[1h]) # DNS hold time p99 (seconds) histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(keen_pbr_dns_hold_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) # Share of set writes slower than 25 ms, per path 1 - sum by (path) (rate(keen_pbr_set_write_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.025"}[5m])) / (sum by (path) (rate(keen_pbr_set_write_duration_seconds_count[5m])) > 0) # Errors in the last hour by subsystem sum by (subsystem) (increase(keen_pbr_errors_total[1h])) > 0
data.configuration#Configuration:
In the web interface, open Security > Authentication and CORS. Turn on Enable authentication, enter a New password and confirm it. If a website on another address must call the API from a browser, add its address to Allowed CORS origins (one per line). Changes take effect immediately.
Set the device name in General > Settings > General > Device name. It appears in the browser tab title and under the keen-pbr logo, which helps tell several routers apart.
The same settings in config.json:
config.json{ "device_name": "Home router", "api": { "enabled": true, "listen": "0.0.0.0:12121", "authentication": { "enabled": true, "password_hash": "argon2id$v=19$m=2048,t=2,p=1$..." }, "cors": { "allowed_origins": ["https://panel.example.com"] } } } device_name is optional and may be empty.
If you edit config.json by hand, generate the password hash with this command (it asks for the password):
keen-pbr hash-password To write the hash straight into the file, run keen-pbr --config /path/to/config.json hash-password --update. Then restart the keen-pbr service: the daemon does not notice changes made to the file from outside.
The password is stored as an Argon2id hash. Hashes from older keen-pbr versions do not work: set the password again.
When authentication is on, requests to the API use one of two methods:
Basic authentication: username admin and your password (curl -u admin:password ...). Bearer token: a temporary key issued by POST /api/auth/login and sent in the header Authorization: Bearer . A token is valid for 24 hours. Only one token is valid at a time: a new login, including one in the web interface, cancels the previous one. After the daemon restarts, get a new token. Without logging in, only GET /api/auth/status and POST /api/auth/login are available. /metrics is protected like the rest of the API.
When authentication is off, requests from other websites in a browser are blocked. When it is on, addresses from Allowed CORS origins are allowed, as well as Chrome and Firefox extensions. The password travels over the network in clear text, so use a trusted network or HTTPS through a reverse proxy (a web server in front of keen-pbr).
By default, the API listens on 0.0.0.0:12121 (api.listen). All routes are served at that address.
The OpenAPI document is the complete request and response schema. The main routes are listed below (an outbound is a channel that traffic goes through: a VPN interface, your ISP, or a block):
Route Purpose GET /api/health/service Service, config draft, current start/stop operation, and rollback status. POST /api/service/start, /stop, /restart Start, stop, or restart routing asynchronously. GET /api/config, POST /api/config Read or stage a validated config draft. GET /api/config/defaults Default values for settings that are not set in the config. POST /api/config/discard, /save, /rollback Discard a draft, save and apply it, or return to the previous config after a failed apply. GET /api/status/events Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream: the server pushes changes, so you do not need to poll. Events: snapshot (full state on connect), service, outbounds, interfaces, issues, routing, auth, config. A keep-alive signal arrives every 15 seconds. The config event carries only a revision number; read the data with GET /api/config. After a dropped connection, the new connection starts with a fresh snapshot. GET /api/health/issues Detected problems and kernel check results: the same list as the overview page and keen-pbr status. GET /api/runtime/outbounds, /api/runtime/interfaces Current outbound state and the list of system interfaces. GET /api/health/routing, POST /api/routing/test Routing and firewall diagnostics, and a route check for a specific domain or IP address. POST /api/lists/refresh Refresh one or all remote URL lists. GET /api/dns/test Stream of DNS and TLS/QUIC interception events, or the DNS check in the web interface. GET /api/diagnostics/command-failure Log of recent system command failures. GET /metrics Prometheus text metrics. /api/auth/status, /api/auth/login, /api/auth/logout, /api/auth/password, /api/auth/settings Authentication status, login and logout, password (GET shows whether one is set; POST sets a new one), and authentication and CORS settings.
data.error-response-400--no-draft#Error Respo:
{ "error": "No staged config to save" } Other errors: 400 (the draft failed validation), 409 (another operation is already running), 500.
After 202, watch the lifecycle_operation field in GET /api/health/service, or subscribe to /api/status/events, until the operation finishes.
If applying failed after the file was saved, GET /api/health/service shows rollback_available: true. The file stays new. To return to the previous config, call POST /api/config/rollback (409 if there is nothing to roll back or another operation is running). POST /api/config/discard only drops an unsaved draft; it changes neither the file nor routing.
data.errors#Errors: keen_pbr_errors_total{subsystem} counts errors by subsystem. All values are always present, zeros included: firewall_apply (applying firewall rules), netlink (setting up routes), set_write (writing addresses to sets), conntrack, dns_parse (parsing DNS packets), dns_tcp_partial (incomplete DNS-over-TCP messages) and dns_late_write (failed deferred writes after a DNS answer).
data.get-apiconfig#GET /api/config:
Returns the current configuration and a flag showing whether an unsaved draft exists. The api settings (password, CORS) are not included. The response also contains list refresh state.
bashcurl http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/config
data.get-apidnstest#GET /api/dns/test:
Streams interception events as Server-Sent Events (the server sends events as they happen). HELLO comes first. The DNS check in the web interface uses this stream: it requests a special marker domain (check.keen-pbr.fyi) and waits for it to appear in the stream.
show=keen-pbr (default): only marker events. The stream closes when the matching marker arrives. Pass domain= to keep your check separate from others. show=all (or show=full): the stream stays open and shows DNS queries, TLS SNI , HTTP Host, QUIC Initial and markers, including domains that are not in any list. show=all exposes the traffic of every client, so it works only when API authentication is on. Without it the response is 403. The default view is always available. An invalid show or domain returns 400.
bashcurl -N -u admin:password 'http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/dns/test?show=all'
data.get-apihealthrouting#GET /api/health/rou:
Returns a report on whether routes and the firewall are set up correctly: firewall rules with packet marks (an fwmark is a number the kernel uses to pick a route), route tables, and the rules that select a table. The report is refreshed in the background, so right after startup it may briefly show an incomplete result.
bashcurl http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/health/routing
data.get-apihealthservice#GET /api/health/ser:
Returns the running daemon version and routing runtime status.
bashcurl http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/health/service
data.get-apiruntimeoutbounds#GET /api/runtime:
Returns the current state of outbounds: which channel a urltest group has selected right now (the group picks the channel with the lowest latency on its own), whether an interface is reachable, and whether it was switched off after a series of failures.
bashcurl http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/runtime/outbounds
data.get-metrics#GET /metrics:
Returns metrics in Prometheus text format 0.0.4. Prometheus requests this address periodically (a scrape) and stores the values. Authentication is the same as for the API: use Basic authentication or the current Bearer token. If metrics are unavailable, the response is 503:
curl -u admin:password http://127.0.0.1:12121/metrics All durations are in seconds (fractional numbers). If a value is unknown, the metric is omitted instead of being exported as 0 (see “Omitted series” below).
data.grafana-dashboard-and-alerts#Grafana das:
Import keen-pbr-dashboard.json into Grafana (Dashboards > New > Import). It needs a Prometheus data source with UID prometheus. The dashboard has job and outbound variables, a 30 s refresh, and the sections Status, Outbounds, DNS interception, Sets & lists and Errors. Use a scrape interval of 30 s or less: the bar panels compute increase() over one-minute windows.
Example alerting rules:
groups: - name: keen-pbr rules: - alert: KeenPbrDown expr: up{job="keen-pbr"} == 0 for: 2m - alert: KeenPbrOutboundDown expr: keen_pbr_probe_up == 0 for: 5m annotations: summary: "{{ $labels.outbound }} probe is failing ({{ $labels.test_outbound }})" - alert: KeenPbrProbeStale # Probes stopped completing (probe interval must be well below 30m). expr: increase(keen_pbr_probe_attempts_total[30m]) == 0 for: 10m - alert: KeenPbrErrors expr: sum by (subsystem) (increase(keen_pbr_errors_total[10m])) > 0 for: 5m - alert: KeenPbrDnsHoldSlow # 0.03 s is the default hold deadline (intercept hold_timeout_ms: 30). expr: > histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(keen_pbr_dns_hold_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 0.03 for: 10m - alert: KeenPbrQueueOverruns expr: sum by (queue) (increase(keen_pbr_queue_overruns_total[10m])) > 0 - alert: KeenPbrListStale expr: time() - keen_pbr_list_last_update_timestamp_seconds > 86400 for: 30m
data.interception#Interception:
Metrics for DNS interception and traffic (L7) analysis. path is dns or l7.
Metric Type Labels Meaning keen_pbr_intercept_packets_total counter path = dns, l7 Packets inspected. keen_pbr_intercept_matches_total counter path = dns, l7 Packets that matched a configured domain list. keen_pbr_dns_hold_duration_seconds histogram - Time a DNS answer was held before its verdict. keen_pbr_dns_queue_wait_duration_seconds histogram - Time a DNS packet waited in the receive queue. keen_pbr_dns_hold_timeouts_total counter cause = batch_budget, admission_blocked, own_write_slow, late_batch_full, other Holds that reached their deadline. keen_pbr_dns_late_writes_total counter - DNS writes completed after the packet was released. keen_pbr_queue_overruns_total counter queue = nfqueue, nflog Kernel queue receive overruns. keen_pbr_set_write_duration_seconds histogram path = dns, late_dns, l7 Dynamic set write time. Buckets (seconds): 0.0001, 0.00025, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.0025, 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, +Inf. keen_pbr_set_writes_total counter kind = add, refresh Elements added (upserted) or timeout-refreshed. keen_pbr_set_refresh_total counter result = skipped, deferred, dropped Cached-element refresh outcomes. dropped means the refresh queue was full. keen_pbr_set_cache_lookups_total counter result = hit, miss Set cache lookups; a hit avoids a write before the verdict. keen_pbr_set_cache_entries gauge - Remembered dynamic set elements. keen_pbr_conntrack_requests_total counter - Conntrack cleanup requests. keen_pbr_conntrack_deleted_total counter - Conntrack entries deleted.
data.omitted-series#Omitted series: probe_up is omitted before the first probe of an outbound completed. probe_latency_seconds, probe_latency_min_seconds and probe_latency_max_seconds are omitted when the last probe failed or no probe completed yet. In Grafana this shows up as a gap, never as a 0. probe_last_success_timestamp_seconds is omitted until the first success. list_last_update_timestamp_seconds and config_reload_last_success_timestamp_seconds are omitted until the first success.
data.post-apiconfig#POST /api/config:
Validates the submitted JSON as a config file and keeps it in memory as a draft. Nothing is written to disk and routing does not change. To save and apply the draft, call POST /api/config/save.
The api field in the request is ignored.
bashcurl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/config \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d @new-config.json
data.post-apiconfigsave#POST /api/config/save:
Starts saving the draft to disk and applying the configuration in the background. 202 means only that the operation was accepted, not that it has finished.
bashcurl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/config/save
data.post-apilistsrefresh#POST /api/lists/ref:
Refreshes remote URL-backed lists from the active daemon config.
If name is provided, only that URL-backed list is refreshed. If name is omitted, all URL-backed lists are refreshed. If list contents changed and that affects routing or DNS, keen-pbr applies the changes immediately. bashcurl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/lists/refresh \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"name":"apple"}' Refresh all URL-backed lists:
bashcurl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/lists/refresh
data.post-apiroutingtest#POST /api/routing/te:
Shows which outbound traffic to a domain or IP address will use. For a domain it first resolves the IP addresses. It then checks the routing rules against the lists (the expected outbound) and the firewall sets (the actual outbound). This helps find a mismatch without restarting the daemon.
bashcurl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12121/api/routing/test \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"target": "example.com", "proto": "tcp", "dest_port": 443}' The optional packet fields (proto: tcp, udp, or other; dest_port, src_addr, src_port, and dscp) let you test rules that filter by port, address, or DSCP . Without them, only list membership of the target is checked.
data.probes-urltest--icmptest#Probes (urltest:
A probe is a periodic check of a channel: a request to a URL (urltest) or a ping (icmptest). Labels: outbound (the channel being checked), test_outbound (the probe group), interface, type (urltest or icmptest).
Metric Type Meaning keen_pbr_probe_attempts_total counter Accepted probe results. keen_pbr_probe_successes_total counter Successful probe results. keen_pbr_probe_packets_sent_total counter ICMP echo requests sent. type="icmptest" only. keen_pbr_probe_packets_received_total counter ICMP echo replies received. type="icmptest" only. keen_pbr_probe_up gauge 1 if the last probe succeeded, 0 if it failed. keen_pbr_probe_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge Unix time of the last successful probe. keen_pbr_probe_latency_seconds gauge Latency of the last successful probe: ICMP is the mean of the received replies, URL is the request time. Sub-millisecond precision. keen_pbr_probe_latency_min_seconds, keen_pbr_probe_latency_max_seconds gauge Fastest and slowest reply of the last successful ICMP probe. type="icmptest" only. keen_pbr_urltest_selected gauge Labels group, outbound: 1 for the group’s currently selected outbound, 0 for the other members. keen_pbr_urltest_selection_changes_total counter Label group: selection changes since the config was last applied (the counter resets on apply).
data.process-and-configuration#Process and co: Metric Type Labels Meaning keen_pbr_build_info gauge version, commit, firewall_backend Always 1; build identity. keen_pbr_process_start_time_seconds gauge - Unix start time; uptime is time() - keen_pbr_process_start_time_seconds. keen_pbr_active_rules gauge - Number of applied firewall rules. keen_pbr_config_reload_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge - Unix time of the last completed config apply (startup counts). Omitted until the first one. keen_pbr_config_reload_errors_total counter - Failed config reloads and applies (parse, validation, prepare or apply failures). keen_pbr_list_last_update_timestamp_seconds gauge list Unix time of the last successful check of a remote (URL) list, whether or not its content changed. Omitted until the first successful refresh after startup. keen_pbr_list_update_errors_total counter list Failed refresh attempts of a remote list.
data.request-body-optional#Request Body (opti: { "name": "apple" } name (optional string): List name to refresh.
data.response#Response:
{ "version": "3.4.0", "build": "20261010120000", "status": "running", "runtime_state": "running", "runtime_state_reason": "config apply complete", "os_type": "debian", "os_version": "12", "build_variant": "generic", "config_is_draft": false, "rollback_available": false } status is running, degraded (DNS interception is enabled but unavailable) or stopped.
When interception is enabled, the response includes an intercept object: whether DNS interception (dns_hold_active) and traffic analysis (l7_active) are active, the kernel features available (nfqueue, nflog, connbytes, addrtype), and counters of processed packets, errors and queue overruns ( NFQUEUE /NFLOG). These values are mostly useful for diagnostics.
For channel state (health, latency) see GET /api/runtime/outbounds.
data.response-1#Response: { "config": { "daemon": { "pid_file": "/var/run/keen-pbr.pid", "cache_dir": "/var/cache/keen-pbr" }, "outbounds": [], "lists": {}, "route": {} }, "is_draft": false, "list_refresh_state": {} } is_draft is true when a config was submitted via POST /api/config but not yet saved to disk.
data.response-200#Response (200):
{ "status": "ok", "message": "Lists refreshed and runtime reloaded", "refreshed_lists": ["apple", "google"], "changed_lists": ["apple"], "failed_lists": [], "reloaded": true } Success payload fields:
refreshed_lists (array[string]): URL-backed lists that were refreshed. changed_lists (array[string]): Refreshed lists whose cached contents changed. failed_lists (array[string]): URL-backed lists that could not be refreshed. reloaded (boolean): Whether the changes were applied because the changed lists are in use.
data.response-3#Response: { "outbounds": [ { "tag": "vpn", "type": "interface", "status": "healthy", "interfaces": [ { "outbound_tag": "vpn", "interface_name": "tun0", "status": "active" } ] }, { "tag": "auto_select", "type": "urltest", "status": "healthy", "interfaces": [ { "outbound_tag": "vpn", "interface_name": "tun0", "status": "active" }, { "outbound_tag": "vpn2", "interface_name": "tun1", "status": "backup" } ] } ] } type: interface, table, blackhole, ignore, urltest or icmptest. Outbound status: healthy (working), degraded (partly working), unavailable (no usable path), unknown. status in interfaces: active (traffic goes through it), backup (standby), degraded, unavailable (switched off after a series of failures), unknown. In a urltest group the selected channel is active. Optional fields: latency_ms, probe_target, detail and packet counters.
data.response-4#Response: { "target": "example.com", "is_domain": true, "resolved_ips": ["93.184.216.34"], "results": [ { "ip": "93.184.216.34", "expected_outbound": "vpn", "actual_outbound": "vpn", "ok": true, "list_match": { "list": "my_domains", "via": "domain" } } ], "warnings": [], "rule_diagnostics": [], "no_matching_rule": false } ok means the expected and actual outbound match. Instead of an outbound name you may see (default) (no rule matched, traffic uses the default) or (unknown) (could not be determined). warnings holds non-fatal warnings, for example a DNS error. rule_diagnostics is a per-rule breakdown (shown in the web interface). no_matching_rule is true when no rule matched.
data.response-5#Response:
{ "overall": "ok", "firewall_backend": "iptables", "firewall": { "chain_present": true, "prerouting_hook_present": true, "verification_state": "verified", "detail": "ok" }, "firewall_rules": [ { "set_name": "", "action": "mark", "expected_fwmark": "0x00010000", "actual_fwmark": "0x00010000", "status": "ok" } ], "route_tables": [ { "table_id": 150, "outbound_tag": "vpn", "expected_interface": "tun0", "expected_gateway": "10.8.0.1", "table_exists": true, "default_route_present": true, "interface_matches": true, "gateway_matches": true, "status": "ok" } ], "policy_rules": [ { "fwmark": "0x00010000", "fwmask": "0x00ff0000", "expected_table": 150, "priority": 1000, "rule_present_v4": true, "rule_present_v6": true, "status": "ok" } ] } firewall.verification_state is verified, unavailable (firewall data not available) or failed. firewall.detail is ok on success and describes the cause otherwise. The optional warnings array lists warnings (for example, NAT is not set up or strict rp_filter is on); they do not affect overall.
Overall status values:
ok — all checks passed degraded — one or more checks failed error — an exception prevented checks from completing Check status values:
ok — check passed missing — expected element not found in kernel mismatch — element found but configuration differs
data.status--error-behavior#Status / Error Be:
200: Refresh operation completed. 400: Requested list exists but is not URL-backed. 404: Requested list not found. 409: Refresh rejected: there is an unsaved config draft or another operation is already running. Error response body:
{ "error": "human-readable message" }

data:
Start with the General > Dashboard page in the web interface: it shows whether the service is running and what exactly is broken. If that is not enough, read the system log: keen-pbr writes the reason for every error there.
Each section below follows the same order: symptom, check in the web interface, check by command, fix.
data.checking-the-resolver-on-the-router#Chec:
Check that the router’s resolver answers locally:
bashnslookup google.com 127.0.0.1 If you see Connection refused, the resolver is not running or is not listening on 127.0.0.1:53. Check its service and log: Entware dnsmasq on Keenetic, dnsmasq on OpenWrt and Debian, or the built-in Keenetic DNS proxy.
On Keenetic, if client DNS queries do not reach Entware dnsmasq, check the opkg dns-override setting. The commands opkg dns-override and system configuration save are run in the router’s web console at http://my.keenetic.net/a, not over SSH. Details are in installing on Keenetic.
After upgrading from an older keen-pbr version After the upgrade, dnsmasq management stays enabled; see Upgrading from 3.3.x. If dnsmasq does not start after you removed keen-pbr manually, make sure its configuration has no leftover conf-script=...keen-pbr... line.
data.diagnostics-messages#Messages in Diagnos:
The Diagnostics panel on the Dashboard page lists the problems found. The Restart button in the status bar re-applies the settings.
Message What to do “Firewall chain is missing”, “Firewall chain is not hooked into PREROUTING” Click Restart in the status bar. If the message stays, read the log: the cause is usually missing permissions or missing iptables / nftables packages. “Firewall rules do not match: N”, “Routing tables do not match: N”, “Policy rules do not match: N” Click Restart. If the message comes back, another program is changing the rules: see “Low-Level Routing Conflicts”. “{tag} is unavailable”, “{tag} is degraded”, “{tag}: failing members: N” The channel {tag} does not answer the health checks. See “Interfaces and VPN Tunnels”. “dnsmasq is not running”, “dnsmasq does not serve the DNS rules”, “DNS rules are being repaired” See “Per-list DNS servers do not work”. “Kernel module is missing and the current rules need it: the firewall rules cannot be applied” Rules that need the module will not be applied until the module is present on the system. “Traffic interception is limited” Look at the state in the Domain-based routing panel and read the log. “Routing checks failed” Click Restart and read the log. “{interface}: no NAT (MASQUERADE/SNAT) for this WAN” Outgoing traffic leaves through this interface without address translation, and replies do not come back. Enable NAT on the interface. For iptables, for example: iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o -j MASQUERADE. If NAT is set up in native nftables rules, you can ignore the warning. “{interface}: strict rp_filter may drop replies” Set the kernel parameters net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf..rp_filter to 2 or 0, for example sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=2. “A foreign rule uses packet mark bits reserved for keen-pbr” Another program uses the packet marks that keen-pbr needs. Open General > Settings > Advanced routing settings (the card is visible when Settings mode = Advanced) and change fwmark starting value and fwmark mask to a free range.
data.dns-interception#DNS interception:
For domain-based routing, keen-pbr reads the DNS answers that pass through the router and remembers the addresses of sites from your lists. No separate DNS server is needed for this.
Symptom: sites do not go through the VPN by domain, but do by IP address.
In the web interface. On the Dashboard page, in the Domain-based routing panel, find the rows DNS interception, DNS hold and L7 interception. The status “Not running” or “Disabled” explains why interception does not work. Below, click Check again in the DNS check widget and compare the result:
“DNS interception from this browser is working”: everything is fine. “Browser request completed, but the interceptor did not see the marker lookup.”: the browser reaches DNS bypassing the router. Turn off encrypted DNS (DoH) in the browser and try again. “DNS interception is disabled in config.”: turn on Intercept DNS server responses in General > Settings > Domain-based routing. “Interception is not working: the DNS hold is not active”: click Restart in the status bar, then read the log. “The browser could not open the live DNS event stream…”: close extra keen-pbr tabs and try again. To check another device, click Test from another device. The dialog shows a command nslookup .check.keen-pbr.fyi: run it on a phone or computer. If “DNS request from the device was observed by the interceptor.” appears, the device uses the router’s DNS. If it says “The DNS test query has not arrived yet…”, make sure the device uses the router’s DNS and run the command again.
Command. On the user’s device:
bashnslookup check.keen-pbr.fyi The domain also has a public address, so the answer shows what happened:
127.0.0.88: the query went through the router and keen-pbr saw it. Any other address: DNS works but bypasses the router. For example, the browser or OS uses its own encrypted DNS. No answer or an error: DNS does not work on the device, or the router’s resolver does not respond.
data.firewall-and-keenpbrtable#Firewall and \:
Symptom: DNS works, the domain resolves, but traffic bypasses the VPN.
In the web interface. In the Diagnostics panel, look for messages about the chain, firewall rules and policies (see the message list above).
Command. The main check:
bashkeen-pbr status Lines with the statuses MISSING, MISMATCH or ERROR in the Firewall block show what is missing.
Look at the firewall rules directly keen-pbr creates its own chain or table KeenPbrTable. Traffic enters it, is matched against the lists, and gets a packet mark ( fwmark ), which the system uses to choose a routing table.
iptables / ipsetnftables / nftsetDebian bashiptables-save | grep KeenPbrTable ip6tables-save | grep KeenPbrTable There should be a jump from PREROUTING to KeenPbrTable and rules with MARK. An example of a correct rule:
-A KeenPbrTable -m set --match-set dst -j MARK --set-xmark / To check the contents of a set:
bashipset list ipset test Expected answer: the IP is in the given set.
bashnft -t list ruleset For the full output including set contents:
bashnft list ruleset There should be a table inet KeenPbrTable, a prerouting hook, rules that check sets, and the action meta mark set ....
The backend depends on how the firewall is installed on your system. Check both variants, or the one named in the keen-pbr log.
bashiptables-save | grep KeenPbrTable ip6tables-save | grep KeenPbrTable nft -t list ruleset Fix. If KeenPbrTable is missing, click Restart in the status bar and read the log. The cause is usually an unavailable backend, missing permissions, missing packages, or a configuration error.
data.interfaces-and-vpn-tunnels#Interfaces an:
Symptom: DNS, firewall and routing look right, but traffic does not go through the VPN.
In the web interface. Open General > Dashboard and look at the Outbounds panel: the channel should be “Healthy”, and its interface “Active” or “Backup”.
Commands.
Check that the interface exists and is up: baship link show ip addr show ip route Check egress through a specific VPN interface: bashcurl -v --interface https://ifconfig.co/json Normally curl returns the VPN’s external IP. If the command hangs or fails, the problem is not in keen-pbr: the tunnel is down, there is no route, the gateway is unreachable, or outgoing traffic is blocked. Fix the VPN itself.
If you use urltest or icmptest urltest and icmptest are outbounds that choose the best of several channels by probing them on a schedule.
Check that the channels (outbounds from outbound_groups) have the right interfaces or tables. Look at the state of each channel in the Outbounds panel on the Dashboard page or on the Routing > Outbounds page. If a channel is “Unavailable”, keen-pbr excluded it after failed probes. Wait for circuit_breaker.timeout_ms or fix the channel. If a backup channel does not take over, first check each channel separately with curl --interface.
data.low-level-routing-conflicts#Low-Level Ro:
If another program on the router also sets packet marks ( fwmark ) or manages ip rule, packets can go the wrong way or be dropped. The message “A foreign rule uses packet mark bits reserved for keen-pbr” in the Diagnostics panel warns about this.
Check for conflicts:
bashkeen-pbr status ip rule show ip route show table all For firewall rules with marks:
iptables / ipsetnftables / nftsetDebian bashiptables-save | grep -E 'MARK|CONNMARK|KeenPbrTable' ip6tables-save | grep -E 'MARK|CONNMARK|KeenPbrTable' bashnft -t list ruleset | grep -E 'mark|KeenPbrTable' bashiptables-save | grep -E 'MARK|CONNMARK|KeenPbrTable' ip6tables-save | grep -E 'MARK|CONNMARK|KeenPbrTable' nft -t list ruleset | grep -E 'mark|KeenPbrTable' Pick a free mark range. In the web interface open General > Settings > Advanced routing settings (the card is visible when Settings mode = Advanced) and change fwmark starting value and fwmark mask. In JSON it looks like this:
config.json{ "fwmark": { "start": "0x00020000", "mask": "0x00FF0000" } } The mask must consist of consecutive hexadecimal F digits. Values are hex strings, for example "0x00FF0000" and "0x00020000".
data.measuring-losses-in-dns-interception#Mea:
For advanced users If the first connection to a freshly opened site sometimes bypasses the VPN, you can measure how often keen-pbr fails to remember the address before the DNS answer reaches the device. The script dns-bench.py does this. It is not included in the keen-pbr packages: download it from the repository. It needs Python 3. Run it from a computer on the local network:
bashpython3 dns-bench.py --api http://192.168.1.1:12121 --password 'admin-password' \ --rates 50,200,1000 --count 1000 The script queries random names like a1b2c3d4-198-18-7-9.nip.io. They point to the test addresses 198.18.0.0/15, so ordinary traffic is not affected. For keen-pbr to process them, add a list and a rule to the configuration (if they are missing, the script tells you what to add):
"lists": { "dns_bench": { "domains": ["nip.io"] } }, "route": { "rules": [ { "list": ["dns_bench"], "outbound": "" } ] } The public nip.io service may rate-limit requests; then client-timeout appears in the report.
Main results in the report:
Result Meaning held-ok All good: the address was recorded before the answer went to the device hold-timeout keen-pbr was not done within intercept.dns.hold_timeout_ms: the answer went out first and the address was added slightly later. The first packets could bypass the VPN set-error The address could not be written to the set; see the keen-pbr log bypass The answer bypassed keen-pbr: the name is not in the lists or the queue overflowed not-in-set, wrong-set After the run the address is not in the set, or is in the set of another outbound client-timeout The device got no answer If there are many hold-timeout results, the router lacks CPU to record addresses. Increase DNS hold timeout (milliseconds) in General > Settings > Domain-based routing. python3 dns-bench.py --help lists all script options.
data.per-list-dns-servers-do-not-work#Per-lis:
Symptom: domains from a list should resolve through the chosen DNS server, but resolve through the default one.
In the web interface.
Open General > Settings > Local DNS server management and make sure Manage dnsmasq configuration is on. On the Dashboard page, look at the DNS Rules panel. “In sync” means everything is applied. “Applying” and “Reconciling” are temporary. For “Error”, look at “Last error” and the message under it: it names the cause and suggests what to do. For example, if it says “Apply or Restart re-arms automatic repair”, click one of them. If you have several dnsmasq instances, pick the right one in the dnsmasq instance field in the same card. Command.
bashkeen-pbr dnsmasq detect The command shows the dnsmasq instances found, their DNS addresses, and the instance keen-pbr uses. In a healthy state keen-pbr is shown as installed, and the problem line says none. If dnsmasq is not installed and you do not need per-list DNS servers, turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration. Otherwise install dnsmasq.
Fix.
If several dnsmasq instances are found, pick the right one in dnsmasq instance and apply the configuration. Make sure clients really use dnsmasq as their resolver. On Keenetic check opkg dns-override (see installing on Keenetic). From a client: bashnslookup example.com If the DNS server has a channel set (detour, for example vpn), make sure this outbound is “Healthy” in the Outbounds panel. Make sure the domains are really in the list. Check them in Routing > Lists and DNS > DNS Rules.
data.quick-check-in-the-web-interface#Quick c:
Open http://:12121/ and go to General > Dashboard.
The status bar at the top. “Everything works” means there are no problems. “Service is stopped” means routing is off: click Start. “System is running, but there are N problems” or “Routing works with limitations” means you should look at the Diagnostics panel. The Outbounds panel. An outbound is a channel that traffic goes through: a VPN interface, your ISP, or a block. Each channel should be “Healthy”. “Degraded” means the channel works partially, “Unavailable” means it does not work. The Diagnostics panel. If everything is fine it says “No problems”. To see healthy items too, turn on Show healthy. For what each message means, see Messages in Diagnostics. The Where does this traffic go? button (Ctrl+Alt+K) in the page header. Enter a domain or IP address and click Check route: keen-pbr shows which rule matches and which outbound the traffic takes. The Domain-based routing panel with the DNS check widget. Click Check again: “DNS interception from this browser is working” means DNS is fine. The same overview is available on the router:
bashkeen-pbr status It prints the state of outbounds, firewall rules, the kernel, DNS interception and dnsmasq, then the list of problems. The Overall: line at the end is the summary. The exit code is 1 if a check failed. The statuses MISSING, MISMATCH and ERROR show what exactly is wrong.
If you cannot solve the problem yourself, click Download report in the Diagnostics panel and attach the file to your request. The report contains your configuration, so read the “Warning: sensitive data” notice first. The option “Hide list contents and list URLs” removes list contents from the report.
data.remote-lists-do-not-update#Remote Lists:
Symptom: a list with a url is empty or outdated.
In the web interface. Open Routing > Lists and click Update next to the list, or Update all. If the button is inactive, apply the draft configuration first.
Command. On the router or server:
bashkeen-pbr download Fix.
Check that the URL is reachable from this same system. If the list must be downloaded through the VPN, check lists[].detour and the matching outbound. If automatic update is used, check Refresh schedule in General > Settings > Lists autoupdate. If a list failed to download at the first start, keen-pbr keeps retrying in the background: after 10 seconds, 30 seconds, 2 minutes, then every 5 minutes, until the download succeeds. If the domain of the list server must resolve through a separate DNS server, add that domain to an inline list, a file list, or an already cached list, otherwise the first attempt goes through the default DNS. After a failure, read the keen-pbr log. Forced full reload This command downloads all remote lists again and re-applies the rules:
Keenetic / NetCrazeOpenWrtDebian bash/opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr reload bashservice keen-pbr reload bashsystemctl reload keen-pbr Also make sure daemon.cache_dir is writable.
data.routing-tables-and-fwmark#Routing Tables:
Symptom: the firewall sets a packet mark ( fwmark ), but the site loads forever or opens through your ISP. The system must see the mark, apply an ip rule, and send the packet to the routing table of the right outbound.
In the web interface. In the Diagnostics panel, look for “Routing tables do not match” and “Policy rules do not match”.
Commands.
Check the state keen-pbr expects: bashkeen-pbr status Check a specific domain or IP. The expected and actual outbound should match: bashkeen-pbr test-routing google.com Check the ip rule entries. There should be a rule like fwmark lookup : baship rule show Check the routing table. It should contain a route through the right VPN interface or gateway. For a blocking outbound (blackhole), expect a blackhole route: baship route show table Fix. If the table is empty, the interface is not found, or the rule points the wrong way, click Restart in the status bar. If that does not help, check the outbound name and interface name, and mark conflicts (see “Low-Level Routing Conflicts”).
data.rules-with-port-or-address-filters-do-no:
When using negation in src_addr / dest_addr fields, the negation applies to all IP addresses/subnets specified in that field. You cannot mix negated and non-negated entries in the same list. Create two separate rules instead.
The same applies to src_port / dest_port.
If rules are not matching as expected:
Make sure the protocol is set correctly: any (null in JSON), "tcp", "udp", or "tcp/udp". Check that the list name in the rule exactly matches the key in lists, including case. Click Where does this traffic go? on the Dashboard page, set Protocol, Destination port and the device IP as in the rule, and look at the result. keen-pbr test-routing does the same, with the options --proto, --src-addr, --src-port, --dest-port, --dscp. Run keen-pbr status and check whether firewall rules were created for this routing rule.
data.service-does-not-start#Service Does Not:
Symptom: the web interface does not open, or the status bar shows “Service is stopped”.
In the web interface: if it opens, click Start or Restart in the status bar on the Dashboard page. If it does not open, use the commands.
Commands. Do not edit the configuration blindly: check the status first and read the log.
Keenetic / NetCrazeOpenWrtDebian Make sure the configuration exists: bashls -l /opt/etc/keen-pbr/config.json Restart keen-pbr: bash/opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr restart Check the keen-pbr status: bash/opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr status Read the system log: bashndmc -c "show log once" | grep -E 'keen-pbr|\[E\]|\[W\]|error|warn|warning' Make sure the configuration exists: bashls -l /etc/keen-pbr/config.json Restart keen-pbr: bashservice keen-pbr restart Check the keen-pbr status: bashservice keen-pbr status Read the system log: bashlogread | grep -E 'keen-pbr|\[E\]|\[W\]|error|warn|warning' Make sure the configuration exists: bashls -l /etc/keen-pbr/config.json Restart keen-pbr: bashsystemctl restart keen-pbr Check the keen-pbr status: bashsystemctl status keen-pbr Read the system log: bashjournalctl -u keen-pbr -b Fix. If keen-pbr does not stay running, stop the service and start keen-pbr manually with verbose logging. The error appears right in the console.
Keenetic / NetCrazeOpenWrtDebian bash/opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr stop keen-pbr --log-level verbose service bashservice keen-pbr stop keen-pbr --log-level verbose service bashsystemctl stop keen-pbr keen-pbr --log-level verbose service While keen-pbr is running, the command does not return to the prompt. That is expected. If it exits right away, the last error in the output is the cause.
Advanced checks Validate the JSON: Keenetic / NetCrazeOpenWrtDebian bashjq . /opt/etc/keen-pbr/config.json bashjq . /etc/keen-pbr/config.json bashjq . /etc/keen-pbr/config.json Make sure the directory for daemon.pid_file exists and is writable. Make sure daemon.cache_dir exists and is writable. If the web interface is enabled, check that the address and port from api.listen are not used by another process. If the log shows a firewall error, check that iptables and ipset, or nftables, are installed for your platform. If keen-pbr is running but the web interface does not open, make sure config.json has an api section.
data.sites-are-not-going-through-the-vpn#Site:
Symptom: a site from a list opens directly instead of through the VPN.
In the web interface.
Click Where does this traffic go? on the Dashboard page, enter the domain and click Check route. To check a specific device, enter its IP in the device IP field. The result tells you what is wrong: “IP not in the expected ipset” (an ipset is a set of addresses that a rule uses to find the right traffic): keen-pbr has not learned the site’s address yet. Open the site on the device, clear the device’s DNS cache, and check that the browser does not use DoH/DoT (encrypted DNS that bypasses the router). “No rule matched. The system route is used.”: the domain is in no list, or the list is not used in a routing rule. Check Routing > Lists and Routing > Routing rules. “The route differs from the expected route”: a rule exists but traffic goes elsewhere. See the firewall and routing table sections below. Make sure the right channel is “Healthy” in the Outbounds panel. Open General > Settings and check three options: Enable domain-based routing (the Domain-based routing card) must be on, otherwise domain rules do not work. IP-based rules work without it. Processed (inbound) interfaces (the General card): if the list is not empty, only traffic from these interfaces is processed, and devices behind other interfaces go directly. Add the LAN interface you need or clear the list. Process router’s own traffic (shown in Advanced settings mode) (the General card) is off by default. Traffic from the router itself, such as curl or ping from the SSH console, is not affected by the rules. Test routing from a device on your local network. Commands. On the router or server:
bashkeen-pbr test-routing google.com The command prints a table: IP address, matched list, expected and actual outbound, and status. To check a specific device, add --src-addr .
Fix. If the expected and actual outbound differ, check in order: DNS (next section), firewall, and routing tables. If they match but the site still does not open through the VPN, check the tunnel itself in “Interfaces and VPN Tunnels”.
data.system-log#System Log:
This is the first place to look. Search for keen-pbr messages and the markers [E] (error) and [W] (warning). If system packages are missing, an interface is not found, the web interface port is taken, or the JSON is broken, the reason is written here.
Keenetic / NetCrazeOpenWrtDebian In the Keenetic web interface, open Diagnostics → System log.
From the console you can read the log like this:
bashndmc -c "show log once" | grep -E 'keen-pbr|\[E\]|\[W\]|error|warn|warning' bashlogread | grep -E 'keen-pbr|\[E\]|\[W\]|error|warn|warning' bashjournalctl -u keen-pbr For the current boot only:
bashjournalctl -u keen-pbr -b
data.tailscale#Routing Breaks When Tailscale:
Tailscale reserves 0x00FF0000, which overlaps the default keen-pbr mask, and restores connmark from conntrack , fully overwriting the packet’s fwmark . Moving keen-pbr to a different fwmark range does not stop Tailscale from erasing it.
Disable Tailscale’s netfilter integration:
bashtailscale set --netfilter-mode=off After that, firewall and NAT rules must be configured separately, especially if Tailscale runs as a subnet router or exit node.
data.urltest-always-shows-degraded#\u003ccode: Make sure the test url is reachable and returns a 2xx code, for example 200 OK or 204 No Content. The default is https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204. If HTTPS probes fail on the router (wrong system time, outdated root certificates, TLS limitations), try an HTTP address, for example http://www.gstatic.com/generate_204. Make sure each channel works on its own. Check the interfaces with curl --interface https://ifconfig.co/json. Wait for the next probe, or temporarily lower interval_ms while diagnosing. Look at the Outbounds panel on the Dashboard page. If a channel is “Unavailable”, keen-pbr excluded it. Wait for circuit_breaker.timeout_ms.
data.websites-are-not-opening-dns_probe_finis: This usually means the resolver is not running or could not apply its configuration. Check the resolver’s service and log: Entware dnsmasq on Keenetic, dnsmasq on OpenWrt and Debian. Then check the Domain-based routing panel on the Dashboard page.

keen-pbr does not answer clients’ DNS queries, so check the resolver your clients use.
Make sure the device uses the router’s DNS. Make sure the router’s resolver has working upstream servers (external DNS it forwards to) and can reach them. Check from the router: nslookup google.com 127.0.0.1. If a DNS server in DNS > DNS servers has a channel set (detour in JSON), check that this outbound is “Healthy” in the Outbounds panel.

data.DNS over TLS: DoT DNS over TLS DNS over TLS: encrypted DNS. The router cannot read these queries.

data.Differentiated Services Code Point: DSCP Differentiated Services Code Point A 6-bit field in the IP header used to mark traffic classes for QoS.
data.Entware: Entware Entware A package repository for routers. On Keenetic, keen-pbr and dnsmasq are installed from it.
data.Internet Control Message Protocol: ICMP Internet Control Message Protocol Service protocol for network diagnostics. ping uses ICMP Echo.
data.MASQUERADE: MASQUERADE MASQUERADE A NAT rule that replaces the source address with the address of the outgoing interface.
data.NAT: NAT NAT Network Address Translation: rewriting packet addresses, for example replacing LAN addresses with the router's WAN address.
data.NFLOG: NFLOG NFLOG A netfilter mechanism that sends copies of packets to a user-space program without delaying them.
data.NFQUEUE: NFQUEUE NFQUEUE A netfilter mechanism that passes packets to a user-space program and waits for its verdict. keen-pbr uses it to hold DNS replies briefly.
data.PREROUTING: PREROUTING PREROUTING The firewall hook that sees incoming packets before the routing decision. keen-pbr sets fwmarks here.
data.QUIC: QUIC QUIC A transport protocol over UDP used by HTTP/3.
data.Quality of Service: QoS Quality of Service Traffic prioritization, for example giving calls priority over downloads.
data.RCI: RCI RCI The Keenetic router's built-in configuration API.
data.Round-trip time: RTT Round-trip time Time from sending a request until its reply arrives.
data.Server Name Indication: SNI Server Name Indication The site name a client sends unencrypted at the start of a TLS connection.
data.Time To Live: TTL Time To Live How long a DNS answer may be cached, in seconds.
data.connmark: connmark connmark Connection mark: a mark stored on a conntrack entry. keen-pbr copies the fwmark into it so every packet of a connection follows the same route.
data.conntrack: conntrack conntrack Connection tracking: the Linux kernel's table of open connections. Each entry can carry its own mark (connmark).
data.drop-in: drop-in drop-in A small extra configuration file that a program reads in addition to its main config.
data.fwmark: fwmark fwmark Firewall mark: a number the Linux kernel attaches to a packet. keen-pbr sets it in the firewall, and ip rule uses it to pick a routing table.
data.ipset: ipset ipset A named set of IP addresses or subnets in the Linux kernel, used by iptables rules to match many addresses at once.
data.mangle: mangle mangle The iptables table for changing packet metadata, such as setting a fwmark, before routing.
data.netfilter: netfilter netfilter The packet filtering framework in the Linux kernel. iptables and nftables are its user-space tools.
data.netlink: netlink netlink The Linux kernel interface programs use to read and change routes, rules, sets and other network settings.
data.network namespace: network namespace network namespace An isolated copy of the Linux network stack with its own interfaces, routes and firewall.
data.nftset: nftset nftset A named set of IP addresses or subnets inside nftables, the nftables counterpart of ipset.
data.policy routing: policy routing policy routing Routing that chooses a routing table by rules (ip rule) instead of only by destination address, for example by fwmark.
data.reverse path filter: reverse path filter reverse path filter A kernel check (rp_filter) that drops a packet if the reply to it would not leave through the interface it arrived on.
